To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

children living in poverty with chronic illness who are also exposed to secondhand smoke are at increased risk of poor health and other adverse health-related outcomes, and the risks are higher than those for children with chronic illness and no secondhand smoke exposure, or children with no chronic illness and secondhand smoke exposure.

families of low-income children with chronic illness and who are exposed to passive smoke have a higher level of risk across multiple domains of the Family Map, including: meeting basic physical, emotional and safety needs, family conflict and stress, parenting stress, parent depression and anxiety.
Children living in poverty who are chronically ill and exposed to second-hand smoke are likely to experience many challenges in addition their chronic illness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the family characteristics of chronically ill children who are exposed to passive smoke and who reside in low-income households.
the effects of chronic illness, passive smoke exposure, and poverty on the health of young children and their families.
identifying family risk and resilience factors for low-income children who are exposed to passive smoke.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study highlights the family risks of a child living with chronic illness, passive smoke and living in poverty.
the children living in poverty with chronic illness who are passive smokers are likely to face more challenges than the children who do not have these conditions.
children who are exposed to both chronic illness and passive smoke are at increased risk for a number of family and environmental risk factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
families of chronically ill children who are exposed to passive smoke have a higher risk of experiencing family conflict, parenting distress, parental depression and anxiety and meeting basic needs.
the children who were chronically ill and exposed to passive smoke had the most family risk.
families of chronically ill children exposed to passive smoke in low-income households are at increased risk for a range of family risks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
families living with chronic illness and exposure to smoke are at a greater risk for family dysfunction than families without either risk factor.
children living in poverty with chronic illness who are also exposed to passive smoke are likely to experience a wide array of family challenges.
the families who are most vulnerable to the negative effects of passive smoke are the families who have the least resources.
